---
title: "Two-part models"
subtitle: "Expected outcomes from a model of whether the outcome is positive and a model of how large it is"
---

A two-part model is used when an outcome is the product of a mix of two
processes, one for observed zeroes and non-zeroes, and one for an amount among
the non-zeroes. The expected outcome is the product of the two:

$$E(y) = \Pr(y > 0) \times E(y \mid y > 0)$$

This is the model the `twopm` command fits (Belotti, Deb, Manning, and Norton
2015). With `suest2`, fit the two parts as separate models, combine them, and
give `margins` the product of the two predictions;
[`mecompare`](../mecompare/examples/two-part.html) automates this calculation
with the `twopart` option.

The examples use the medical expenditures of 19,386 adults in the 2004 Medical
Expenditure Panel Survey. The first part is a logit of whether a person had any
medical expenditures. The second part is a Poisson model of expenditures among
the people who had any. With robust standard errors, `poisson` is Poisson
pseudo-maximum likelihood: it fits a model of the mean of any outcome that is
zero or positive, not only counts, and needs only the model of the mean to be
right (Santos Silva and Tenreyro 2006).

## Fit the two parts and combine them

Both parts cluster on the dwelling unit (`duid`):

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/meps", clear
(MEPS 2004 adults, total medical expenditures (from R package twopartm))

. generate byte any = exp_tot > 0

. tabulate any

        any |      Freq.     Percent        Cum.
------------+-----------------------------------
          0 |      3,440       17.74       17.74
          1 |     15,946       82.26      100.00
------------+-----------------------------------
      Total |     19,386      100.00

. 
. local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

. 
. quietly logit any `x', vce(cluster duid)

. estimates store Any

. 
. quietly poisson exp_tot `x' if any, vce(cluster duid)

. estimates store Amount

. 
. suest2 Any Amount

Simultaneous results for Any, Amount                    Number of obs = 19,386

                                (Std. err. adjusted for 10,940 clusters in duid)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
               |               Robust
               | Coefficient  std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
Any_any        |
           age |      0.030      0.002   19.358   0.000        0.027       0.033
      1.female |      0.957      0.044   21.744   0.000        0.871       1.044
         lninc |      0.349      0.026   13.273   0.000        0.298       0.401
         pcs12 |     -0.040      0.003  -12.130   0.000       -0.046      -0.033
         mcs12 |     -0.016      0.003   -6.430   0.000       -0.021      -0.011
   1.ins_unins |     -1.644      0.050  -32.946   0.000       -1.742      -1.546
      1.anylim |      0.799      0.073   10.991   0.000        0.657       0.942
         _cons |     -0.695      0.342   -2.033   0.042       -1.364      -0.025
---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
Amount_exp_tot |
           age |      0.011      0.001    8.146   0.000        0.008       0.014
      1.female |      0.046      0.039    1.180   0.238       -0.031       0.124
         lninc |      0.066      0.022    3.034   0.002        0.023       0.109
         pcs12 |     -0.036      0.002  -18.391   0.000       -0.040      -0.033
         mcs12 |     -0.012      0.002   -6.746   0.000       -0.015      -0.009
   1.ins_unins |     -0.910      0.064  -14.169   0.000       -1.036      -0.784
      1.anylim |      0.362      0.040    9.146   0.000        0.284       0.439
         _cons |      9.183      0.284   32.360   0.000        8.627       9.739
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

```

With survey data, fit both parts with `svy:` and the second part with `if any`,
not `subpop()`: `suest2` needs the same subpopulation in every model, and it
computes the standard errors from the full survey design.

## Expected expenditures and effects on them

`predict(twopart(Any Amount))` is the product of the two predictions: the
probability of any expenditures from `Any` times the expected expenditures of
someone who has any from `Amount`:

```{.stata-run}
. margins, predict(twopart(Any Amount))

Predictive margins                                      Number of obs = 19,386
Model VCE: Robust

Expression: Two-part prediction, predict(twopart(Any Amount))

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |            Delta-method
             |     Margin   std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
       _cons |   3681.427     64.963   56.670   0.000     3554.102    3808.752
------------------------------------------------------------------------------

. margins, dydx(age female ins_unins anylim) predict(twopart(Any Amount))

Average marginal effects                                Number of obs = 19,386
Model VCE: Robust

Expression: Two-part prediction, predict(twopart(Any Amount))
dy/dx wrt:  age 1.female 1.ins_unins 1.anylim

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |            Delta-method
             |      dy/dx   std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
         age |     48.618      4.961    9.799   0.000       38.894      58.342
    1.female |    416.758    140.808    2.960   0.003      140.779     692.736
 1.ins_unins |  -2700.969    113.169  -23.867   0.000    -2922.777   -2479.161
    1.anylim |   1532.778    151.644   10.108   0.000     1235.562    1829.995
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: dy/dx for factor levels is the discrete change from the base level.

```

Expected expenditures average about $3,680 a year. Being uninsured is
associated with $2,700 less in expenditure; each year of age predicts a $49
increase; being female, a $417 increase; and having any activity limitation, a
$1,533 increase.

## Effects in each part

Naming one model in `predict()` gives the effect in that part alone:

```{.stata-run}
. margins, dydx(ins_unins) predict(model(Any))

Average marginal effects                                Number of obs = 19,386
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |            Delta-method
             |      dy/dx   std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
   ins_unins |
          1  |     -0.242      0.009  -28.369   0.000       -0.259      -0.226
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: dy/dx for factor levels is the discrete change from the base level.

. margins, dydx(ins_unins) predict(model(Amount))

Average marginal effects                                Number of obs = 19,386
Model VCE: Robust

Expression: Predicted mean of exp_tot, predict(model(Amount))
dy/dx wrt:  1.ins_unins

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |            Delta-method
             |      dy/dx   std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
 1.ins_unins |  -2602.641    136.211  -19.107   0.000    -2869.610   -2335.672
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: dy/dx for factor levels is the discrete change from the base level.

```

Being uninsured lowers the probability of any expenditures by 24 percentage
points, and the expected expenditures of someone who has any by about $2,600.
Both are averaged over the whole sample, so the two effects are for the same
people. Adding `if any` averages the amount effect over only the people with
any expenditures, the observations the second part was fit to, as `poisson`
gives it on its own:

```{.stata-run}
. margins if any, dydx(ins_unins) predict(model(Amount))

Average marginal effects                                Number of obs = 15,946
Model VCE: Robust

Expression: Predicted mean of exp_tot, predict(model(Amount))
dy/dx wrt:  1.ins_unins

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
             |            Delta-method
             |      dy/dx   std. err.      z    P>|z|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------
 1.ins_unins |  -2832.947    147.594  -19.194   0.000    -3122.226   -2543.669
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Note: dy/dx for factor levels is the discrete change from the base level.

```

Among the people with any expenditures, being uninsured is associated with
about $2,830 less in expenditure. This describes the people who spend, but it
is averaged over different observations than the first part's effect, so the
two can differ partly because the observations used to calculate the marginal
effect differ.

## How well the model predicts

The correlation between the outcome and its expected value summarizes how well
a two-part model predicts. It depends only on the expected outcome, so it
applies with any second part:

```{.stata-run}
. predict double yhat if e(sample), twopart(Any Amount)

. correlate exp_tot yhat
(obs=19,386)

             |  exp_tot     yhat
-------------+------------------
     exp_tot |   1.0000
        yhat |   0.3916   1.0000


```

The correlation is .392.

## Other second parts and comparisons

The second part can also be a `glm`, such as a gamma family with a log link,
`regress`, or `nbreg`; `predict(twopart())` works the same way with each. With
a regression of the log of the outcome, add `duan` for Duan's (1983) smearing
estimate or `normal` for the normal-theory retransformation, as in
`predict(twopart(Any LnAmount) duan)`. The `mecompare` [Two-part
models](../mecompare/examples/two-part.html) page compares effects across
two-part models with different second parts, and between a two-part model and
a single model for the outcome.
